The shoulders, neck and sides are a lighter gray. The fur around the eyes is whitish. The underside is lighter, buff or grayish yellow. The tail is relatively bushy for a ground squirrel, and at a quick glance, the squirrel might be mistaken for a fox squirrel.
As is typical for ground squirrels, California ground squirrels live in burrows, which they excavate themselves. Some burrows are occupied communally, but each squirrel has its own entrance. Although they readily become tame in areas used by humans, and quickly learn to take food left or offered by picnickers, they spend most of their time within 25 m (80 ft) of their burrows, and rarely go further than 50 m (160 ft) from it.
In the colder parts of their range, California ground squirrels hibernate for several months, but in areas where winters have no snow, most squirrels are active year-round."

The ground squirrels are cute, BUT they’ve chased away the local Chuckwalla lizards that inhabited this hill side. 

California Ground Squirrel (Otospermophilus beecheyi) The "squirrel's upper parts are mottled, with the fur containing a mixture of gray, light brown and dusky hairs. The shoulders, neck and sides are a lighter gray. The fur around the eyes is whitish. The underside is lighter, buff or grayish yellow. Head and body are about 30 cm (12 in) long and the tail an additional 15 centimetres (5.9 in). They can weigh from 280 to 738 g (9.9 to 26.0 oz). The tail is relatively bushy for a ground squirrel, and at a quick glance, the squirrel might be mistaken for a fox squirrel.
As is typical for ground squirrels, California ground squirrels live in burrows, which they excavate themselves. Some burrows are occupied communally, but each squirrel has its own entrance. Although they readily become tame in areas used by humans, and quickly learn to take food left or offered by picnickers, they spend most of their time within 25 m (80 ft) of their burrows, and rarely go further than 50 m (160 ft) from it.
In the colder parts of their range, California ground squirrels hibernate for several months, but in areas where winters have no snow, most squirrels are active year-round."
https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/180007-Otospermophilus-beecheyi

description:
This week when I was walking to the Macoskey Center through the field behind Building F, I saw a brown lump sitting on the ground. Not sure what it was I walked up to it thinking it was just some dead grass. I got a closer look and was able to identify the species as a groundhog (Marmota monax), also commonly referred to as a woodchuck. It was not alive at the time I discovered it, but I could tell it was a groundhog because of it's grizzled brown fur, short ears, round face, short legs, and bushy tail. Presumably the cause of death could have been the groundhog was shot because of blood on the shoulder or the front left leg.. According to the National Audubon Society Field Guide to the Mid-Atlantic States, groundhogs are part of the squirrel family and hibernate during the early winter. To no surprise it also states that their habitat is in fields and woodland edges which makes sense for when my discovery was made.

The temperature has started warming up recently, so many animals have been coming out of hibernation. On the day of the observation the high temperature was 58°F and low of 24°F. When the encounter was made, it was sunny and 32°F, with 88% humidity and winds at 3 mph headed NE.

In an article I read about groundhogs hibernation from Penn State Extension, it mentions that they are one of the most widely distributed mammals in Pennsylvania. It also mentions they have a lifespan of 3 to 4 years. Some of their predators include hawks, foxes, coyotes, and humans, where in most cases they are hit by cars on the road. That was not the case for this one because it was far enough from the road and didn't look to have any signs that it could have been hit. This also leads to the possibility that one of it's predators attacked it, leaving the blood on the leg, but not consuming it. I still want to say it looks more like a gunshot wound though.

In the colder parts of their range, California ground squirrels hibernate for several months, but in areas where winters have no snow, most squirrels are active year-round."

California Ground Squirrel (Otospermophilus beecheyi) The "squirrel's upper parts are mottled, with the fur containing a mixture of gray, light brown and dusky hairs. The shoulders, neck and sides are a lighter gray. The fur around the eyes is whitish. The underside is lighter, buff or grayish yellow. Head and body are about 30 cm (12 in) long and the tail an additional 15 centimetres (5.9 in). They can weigh from 280 to 738 g (9.9 to 26.0 oz). The tail is relatively bushy for a ground squirrel, and at a quick glance, the squirrel might be mistaken for a fox squirrel.
As is typical for ground squirrels, California ground squirrels live in burrows, which they excavate themselves. Some burrows are occupied communally, but each squirrel has its own entrance. Although they readily become tame in areas used by humans, and quickly learn to take food left or offered by picnickers, they spend most of their time within 25 m (80 ft) of their burrows, and rarely go further than 50 m (160 ft) from it.
In the colder parts of their range, California ground squirrels hibernate for several months, but in areas where winters have no snow, most squirrels are active year-round."

description: This groundhog (Marmota monax) hole was found in my backyard after I was too slow to catch a picture of the groundhog. I was inside my house when I spotted the groundhog, but it disappeared quickly! Even if I had not seen the animal, the hole is still identifiable as it has a few characteristics of a typical groundhog hole. Groundhog holes also feature crescent-shaped indents in the dirt. This hole seemed to be around 10 inches in diameter, which is the usual size of their burrows. description: Handled as part of AZGFD population monitoring efforts

It was only after I looked to see how many (or few) other Groundhog sightings have been reported to *iNaturalist* within *Mingo Creek County Park*, that I decided to post this one. The photographs are from a great distance and are not very sharp, but are sufficient for identification. As of September, 2024, this is only the second observation of a live Woodchuck (as we call them here) in the Park, along with one adult skull found four years ago. They are pretty common in southwestern Pennsylvania generally. So, why so few at Mingo Creek? Seems odd. No hunting is allowed within the Park, but these are not considered "game" animals. Some farmers and horse owners consider them pests, and I've heard of them being shot on sight on some properties, but I wouldn't think that goes on in a County Park. 

This one was quite wary of my intruding on its evening grazing on grass in the open, and fled into the high weeds and brush quickly after it spotted me crossing the field toward it. As soon as I could make a couple photos, it was quietly gone. They seem naturally pretty shy, much more so than their arboreal cousins the tree squirrels. I'm not sure why. 

This was fifteen minutes before sundown, at the edge of a large hilltop open field, a grass strip airfield of the *Washington County Model Aviation Association* actually, surrounded by large tracts of dense mixed deciduous woodland.

description:
This "Woodchuck" (as Groundhogs are called here) often climbed this small tree along a tiny creek next to a hay field and would spend time apparently just resting and watching the world go by. On this occasion, he [she?] draped himself restfully on the limb with feet dangling for over a half an hour. I have seen other Woodchucks climb trees and fenceposts briefly for a look around their surroundings, but this guy went up to visibly relax in a place with a panoramic view for extended periods. He had a den in a bank not far from the base of this tree. He climbed other trees in the vicinity, sometimes laying down 2 or 3 meters off the ground. It got so that I expected to see him up a tree whenever I looked down towards that part of the farmyard, for a couple years it seems. He often put his head down and would even sprawl limply as though on a couch. I never bothered him when in these arboreal reveries, but would watch from a discrete distance. 

When descending, he could skillfully climb head down. 

He's gone now, but I always think if him when I walk here and see these trees. 

This was on the edge of a hayfield where a stream bank and a row of trees and brush provide some cover, and adjacent to a mowed yard, on an old sheep and cattle farm established in 1789, in a valley on the Allegheny Plateau. The hills are covered in mixed deciduous woodland, largely Maples, Oaks, Beech, and Hickories.

description: There are numerous prairie dog towns spread throughout the region, including both the north and south units of Theodore Roosevelt National Park.  I don't usually pay them a lot of attention but they do amuse me occasionally with all their chirping squeals/"barks" when they become excited about something.  Black-tailed prairie dogs range from the Plains of southern Canada all the way to Mexico and their burrows have always placed them at odds with ranchers ever since the first settlers pushed west on the continent.  They're highly social and always seem to be chattering back and forth, especially if a predator happens to be near or flying overhead.  (9-3-2023)

description:
Prairie dogs both lounging and standing watch in one of the several prairie dog towns located within Theodore Roosevelt National Park (south unit). There are also prairie dog towns in the north unit, though a hike is required to see them.  Though their numbers have been greatly reduced since settlers arrived in the West (they are still considered a nuisance to ranchers because of the burrows), they are still a fairly common site in this region.  

I was giving a grand tour of both units of the park to a friend of mine that was in Williston over the weekend and we had excellent luck throughout the day at both units, for we saw a large majority of the larger wildlife (with the exception of elk in the south unit, for I seem to possess an elk-repellent system lol).
